blocks.text: At New York’s New Museum, “I Am Tony,” Arthur Jafa’s largest retrospective to date, moves across photography, painting, video and sculpture in pursuit of a “Black Visual Intonation.”
By Gaia Squarci. Artwork by Arthur Jafa.

blocks.caption: HR, 2018. Private collection. © Arthur Jafa. Courtesy the artist and Gladstone

blocks.text: Fifteen years ago, at 50, Arthur Jafa felt like a failure. He had spent decades working as a cinematographer for filmmakers like Julie Dash, Spike Lee and Stanley Kubrick, yet he questioned his place as an artist, and above all as a Black American artist. He sought visual forms that could hold the full reality of Black life in America without reducing it to a single perspective. When his work finally came together, it held pain, beauty, violence and grief.

blocks.caption: AGHDRA, 2021. 4K digital video, color, sound. © Arthur Jafa. Courtesy the artist and Gladstone
Arthur Jafa, La Scala, 2018. © Arthur Jafa. Courtesy the artist and Gladstone

blocks.text: That tension runs through the exhibition like a leitmotif. Visitors move through darkened rooms where photographs juxtapose in a tunnel, hang on a wall beside a real black car, or turn into cutouts. Jafa addresses today’s flood of pictures, sampling and remixing so that each one takes its meaning from its neighbors. Artemisia Gentileschi, Mickey Mouse and Michael Jackson end up next to the 1863 photograph of Gordon (or Peter), the formerly enslaved man whose scarred back became one of the most haunting images of slavery.

Love is the Message, The Message is Death, 2016.  4K digital video, color, sound. © Arthur Jafa. Courtesy the artist and Gladstone

blocks.text: What connects the pieces is Black sound, which changed the history of American music and gives Jafa’s work its emotional rhythm. In the video installation AGHDRA , a sea of molten rock heaves and breaks apart under a setting sun. An ominous sound vibrates in the visitor’s chest, and Jafa calls the piece “a [James] Turrell while you’re chained in the bottom of a boat.” Drawing on history, pop culture and music, his work acts on the body as much as the mind, leaving viewers to ask where they stand.

blocks.caption: Monster, 1988. © Arthur Jafa. Courtesy the artist and Gladstone

blocks.text: The exhibition “I Am Tony” is on view at The New Museum until January 3, 2027.
